stumbles.quote: Jev, a small decision model that returns a calibrated probability for a yes/no question in about 160 ms
stumbles.why: Jev is introduced as a model but never explained further (who made it, how it is used). 'Routing questions' later leans on unstated prior use.

stumbles.quote: I was disappointed when its probabilities clustered between 0.3 and 0.8 instead.
stumbles.why: The link between this clustering and the 24.5% result is never stated. The text also doesn't explain how a '5% error budget' turns probabilities into settled hits, or what 'settle' means.

stumbles.quote: because it had done well on routing questions
stumbles.why: Refers to earlier Jev work that the text never describes, and 'routing' is not defined.
Oskar is not introduced. 'Our public posting review process' is also never described.

stumbles.quote: our advance bar of settling 50% of hits
stumbles.why: The heading calls it 'the 50% bar'. The text never says when or why this bar was set, or why 50% is the threshold.
The file is never explained. The reader can't tell what the 'tic's definition' contains.
'Tic' is never defined. The reader has to infer it means an AI-writing pattern that the linter flags correctly.

stumbles.quote: A baseline that uses only the hit's lint category—its historical tic rate—
stumbles.why: The text doesn't say where the historical rate comes from. If it comes from the same 300 hits, the comparison may be circular. The category names (`negation-first`, `triad`, `participle`) are also unexplained.

stumbles.quote: In the underlying `declaude_lint` rules, 16 of 18 `negation-first` hits
stumbles.why: The counts (18, 44, 43) cover only part of the 261 hits, and the other categories are not shown. The text doesn't say how this per-category breakdown bears on the decision.

point: Jev was only modestly better than a simple per-category baseline at ranking lint hits, and it settled just 24.5% of hits at the 5% error budget, below the 50% bar, so it was not adopted for public posting review.
